title: CSS Modules for Scoped Styles
description: Write styles that only affect one component – no more class name collisions!

slides.title: The Problem: Class Name Collisions 💥
slides.content:
# Imagine...

You have a `.button` class in `Header.css` and another `.button` in `Footer.css`. The last one loaded wins and styles get mixed up.

In large apps, keeping track of unique class names becomes a nightmare.

**CSS Modules** solve this by automatically scoping class names to the component.

File naming: `Button.module.css`

```jsx
import styles from './Button.module.css';
<button className={styles.primary}>Click</button>
```

Next.js compiles the class to something like `Button_primary__abc123`.

slides.title: A Scoped Button (components/Button.js)
slides.content: Import the module and use the generated class names.

quizData.question: What is the main benefit of CSS Modules?

options.text: They automatically scope class names to a component, preventing conflicts
They allow inline styles in JS

quizData.explanation: CSS Modules generate unique class names, so styles are local by default and never clash with others.

slides.title: Composing & Dynamic Styles 🎨
Conditional Styling (components/Alert.js)
slides.content: Use a prop to decide the class.

quizData.question: How do you apply two CSS Module classes to the same element?
quizData.explanation: You concatenate the generated class names with a space, e.g., `${styles.a} ${styles.b}`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 💡
slides.content: CSS Modules are supported out of the box. No config needed. You can also use Sass (`*.module.scss`) if you install `sass`.
